summary: This unit covers where the coronary arteries arise, how they branch, which part of the heart each one feeds, and how the heart's veins drain back to the right atrium. The exam uses it to link a blocked artery to the wall that dies, the ECG leads that change, and the complications that follow.

points: Right coronary artery (RCA) arises from the right aortic sinus; left coronary artery (LCA) from the left aortic sinus.
Left main runs between the pulmonary trunk and left auricle, then splits into the LAD and the circumflex (LCx).
LAD (anterior interventricular artery) runs down the anterior interventricular groove to the apex.
LAD feeds the anterior LV wall, the apex, and the anterior two-thirds of the septum (septal perforators); diagonal branches feed the anterolateral wall.
LCx runs in the left atrioventricular (coronary) groove to the back; obtuse marginal branches feed the lateral LV wall.
notes.why: The left main is short and feeds most of the left ventricle through two branches, so a left main occlusion puts a large mass of myocardium at risk. Because the LAD supplies the anterior wall, apex, and anterior two-thirds of the septum, its occlusion causes an anterior or anteroseptal infarct seen in leads V1 to V4 and can injure the bundle branches that run in the septum. The circumflex travels in the AV groove toward the lateral and posterior wall, so its occlusion produces a lateral infarct seen in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6.

points: RCA runs in the right atrioventricular groove.
Right (acute) marginal branch feeds the right ventricle.
SA nodal artery comes from the RCA in about 60% of hearts and from the LCx in about 40%.
AV nodal artery comes from the RCA in about 80% of hearts.
In a right-dominant heart the RCA gives the posterior descending artery (PDA), which feeds the posterior one-third of the septum and the inferior LV wall.
notes.why: The RCA supplies the right ventricle and, in most hearts, the SA and AV nodes, which is why an RCA occlusion links an inferior infarct (leads II, III, and aVF) to bradycardia and AV block. Inferior wall ischemia also triggers vagal reflexes (the Bezold-Jarisch reflex) that add bradycardia and hypotension. Right ventricular infarction cuts delivery of blood to the left heart, so the patient becomes preload dependent: clear lungs, raised jugular venous pressure, and hypotension that worsens with nitrates.

points: Dominance is defined by which artery gives the PDA.
Most hearts are right dominant (estimates run from about 67% to 85%); the rest are left dominant (PDA from LCx) or codominant.
Anterolateral papillary muscle has a double supply (LAD and LCx).
Posteromedial papillary muscle depends on the PDA alone, so it is the one that ruptures after an inferior MI.
notes.why: The PDA feeds the inferior wall and posterior septum, so the artery that gives rise to it decides which occlusion causes an inferior infarct. The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply with no second source to back it up, so ischemia there progresses to necrosis. Rupture usually comes about 2 to 7 days after the infarct, when macrophages have softened the dead tissue, and causes acute mitral regurgitation with sudden pulmonary edema and a new holosystolic murmur.

points: Coronary sinus lies in the posterior atrioventricular groove and opens into the right atrium.
Great cardiac vein runs with the LAD, middle cardiac vein with the PDA, small cardiac vein with the right marginal artery; all three reach the coronary sinus.
Anterior cardiac veins drain the front of the RV straight into the right atrium.
Smallest cardiac veins (venae cordis minimae) open directly into the chambers.
notes.why: Coronary veins mostly run beside the arteries and converge on the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium near the opening of the IVC. Because a persistent left superior vena cava drains into the coronary sinus, it shows up as a dilated sinus on echocardiography. The smallest cardiac veins empty some deoxygenated blood straight into the left chambers, which, together with the bronchial veins, creates a small normal right-to-left shunt.

points: Resting coronary flow is about 225 mL/min, about 4 to 5% of cardiac output.
LV muscle is perfused mostly in diastole, because systole squeezes the intramyocardial vessels shut.
Tachycardia shortens diastole, so it cuts LV perfusion while raising demand.
The heart extracts about 70% of arterial oxygen at rest, so more demand must be met by more flow.
Adenosine and other local metabolites are the main coronary vasodilators.
The subendocardium has the highest wall stress and the least flow reserve, so it becomes ischemic first.
notes.why: Coronary perfusion depends on the driving pressure (aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure) and on how much of each cycle is spent in diastole. Since resting oxygen extraction is already near its maximum, the heart meets higher demand only by vasodilation: ATP breakdown yields adenosine, which relaxes coronary smooth muscle. A fixed stenosis uses up this reserve, so ischemia appears first in the subendocardium during exercise or tachycardia, producing stable angina and ST depression.

tricks.label: Who gives the PDA wins
tricks.text: To name the dominant artery, ask only one question: which artery gives the posterior descending artery? Size of the vessel does not matter.

tricks.label: Veins shadow arteries
tricks.text: Pair each vein with its artery: great with LAD, middle with PDA, small with right marginal. All three empty into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.

tricks.label: Diastole feeds the left
tricks.text: Anything that shortens diastole (fast heart rate) or lowers aortic diastolic pressure (aortic regurgitation, hypotension) starves the LV subendocardium first.

highYield: LAD is the most commonly occluded coronary artery, followed by the RCA, then the LCx.
Inferior MI (II, III, aVF) usually means RCA occlusion and can come with bradycardia or AV block.
Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture after inferior MI causes sudden acute mitral regurgitation.
Coronary perfusion pressure is aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure.
Coronary sinus runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove and opens into the right atrium.
Adenosine is the classic local metabolite that dilates coronary arterioles when demand rises.
pitfalls: Dominance is about who supplies the PDA; a large LCx can still sit in a right-dominant heart.
The SA node is usually fed by the RCA (about 60%), but in about 40% it comes from the LCx, so an LCx lesion can still cause sinus node problems.
The anterolateral papillary muscle rarely ruptures because it has two arteries; the posteromedial one has only the PDA.
Anterior cardiac veins and smallest cardiac veins bypass the coronary sinus, so the coronary sinus does not carry all cardiac venous blood.

flows.title: Path of coronary blood flow
steps: Blood leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve.
Enters the coronary ostia in the right and left aortic sinuses, mostly in diastole.
Flows through epicardial arteries into intramyocardial arterioles and capillaries.
Most venous blood collects in the great, middle, and small cardiac veins.
Veins join the coronary sinus in the posterior atrioventricular groove.
Coronary sinus empties into the right atrium.

flows.title: Demand ischemia from a fixed stenosis
steps: Exercise raises heart rate and contractility, so myocardial O₂ demand rises.
Extraction is already near maximal, so coronary flow must rise.
Arterioles beyond the stenosis are already dilated, so flow cannot rise enough.
Tachycardia shortens diastole and cuts subendocardial perfusion further.
Subendocardial ischemia causes angina and ST depression.

flows.title: Inferior MI from RCA occlusion
steps: Plaque rupture in a dominant RCA forms an occlusive thrombus.
Inferior LV wall and posterior septum lose PDA flow.
ST elevation appears in leads II, III, and aVF.
AV nodal ischemia and vagal reflexes cause bradycardia or AV block.
Posteromedial papillary muscle necrosis can lead to rupture and acute mitral regurgitation.

summary: This unit covers how arterial blood reaches the head, limbs, and abdominal organs, how venous blood returns, and how the portal system connects the gut to the liver. Exam questions name a vessel or a vertebral level and ask what it supplies, or describe a blockage and ask what tissue suffers.

points: Arch branches, right to left: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian.
Brachiocephalic trunk splits into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.
Common carotid divides at about the level of C4 (upper border of the thyroid cartilage) into internal and external carotids.
Descending thoracic aorta gives posterior intercostal, bronchial, and esophageal branches.
notes.why: The arch is asymmetric because the left fourth pharyngeal arch artery and left dorsal aorta form the definitive arch, while on the right the fourth arch artery forms only the proximal right subclavian and the right horn of the aortic sac becomes the brachiocephalic trunk. The carotid bifurcation holds the carotid sinus baroreceptors and is a favorite site for plaque, because flow separates there and shear stress is low. In coarctation distal to the left subclavian, blood bypasses the narrowing through internal thoracic and intercostal arteries, which notch the ribs, while the legs have weak, delayed pulses.

points: Enters the abdomen through the aortic hiatus at T12 and bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at L4.
Unpaired gut arteries: celiac trunk (T12), superior mesenteric artery (L1), inferior mesenteric artery (L3).
Paired branches: inferior phrenic, middle suprarenal, renal (about L1), gonadal (about L2), and four pairs of lumbar arteries.
Celiac trunk gives the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.
Splenic flexure sits between SMA and IMA territories, a watershed zone for ischemic colitis.
notes.why: The three gut arteries match the embryonic foregut, midgut, and hindgut: the celiac trunk feeds the stomach through the proximal duodenum, the SMA feeds the distal duodenum through the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, and the IMA feeds the rest of the colon to the upper rectum. Where two territories meet with thin collateral links, a fall in perfusion starves the tissue first, which is why ischemic colitis favors the splenic flexure. Most abdominal aortic aneurysms lie below the renal arteries (infrarenal), which arise near L1.

points: Brain gets anterior flow from the internal carotids and posterior flow from the vertebral arteries (branches of the subclavians), which join as the basilar artery.
Circle of Willis links them: anterior communicating, anterior cerebral, internal carotid, posterior communicating, and posterior cerebral arteries.
Upper limb: subclavian becomes axillary at the lateral border of the first rib, then brachial at the lower border of teres major; brachial splits into radial and ulnar in the cubital fossa.

Lower limb: external iliac becomes femoral under the inguinal ligament, then popliteal at the adductor hiatus; popliteal splits into anterior tibial and the tibiofibular trunk (posterior tibial and fibular).
Dorsalis pedis is the continuation of the anterior tibial artery.
notes.why: Paired inflow from the carotids and vertebrals, joined by the circle of Willis, lets collateral flow protect the brain when one inflow narrows slowly, though the communicating arteries vary in size and the cerebral branches beyond the circle overlap little. Limb arteries lie against bone or are tethered at fixed points, so fractures and dislocations at those sites injure them: a supracondylar humerus fracture threatens the brachial artery, and a posterior knee dislocation threatens the popliteal artery, which is tethered at the adductor hiatus. Radial, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses give a bedside check on each path.

points: SVC forms from the two brachiocephalic veins; IVC forms from the common iliac veins at about L5.
Left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta just below the SMA; the left gonadal vein drains into it, while the right gonadal vein drains straight into the IVC.
Hepatic portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins; the inferior mesenteric vein usually joins the splenic vein.
Portal blood passes through liver sinusoids, then leaves by the hepatic veins into the IVC.
notes.why: Because the portal vein drains the gut, absorbed nutrients and oral drugs pass through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation (first-pass metabolism). When portal pressure rises, as in cirrhosis, blood reroutes through portosystemic anastomoses: left gastric to esophageal veins (varices), paraumbilical to superficial abdominal wall veins (caput medusae), and superior rectal to middle and inferior rectal veins. The left renal vein can be compressed between the aorta and SMA (nutcracker syndrome), which backs blood up into the left gonadal vein and can cause a left varicocele.

notes.h: Where cardiac output goes at rest
points: Liver and gut together receive about a quarter of resting cardiac output, kidneys about a fifth.
Skeletal muscle gets about 15% at rest and the brain about 14%.
Heart muscle gets about 4 to 5% but uses oxygen at a very high rate.
notes.why: Organs sit in parallel, so each receives a share of output set by its own resistance. The kidneys get flow far above their oxygen needs because they must filter plasma, so renal venous blood stays well oxygenated, while the heart gets little flow but extracts most of its oxygen, so coronary sinus blood is the most deoxygenated venous blood in the body. In shock, sympathetic constriction shifts flow away from the gut, kidneys, skin, and resting muscle to protect the brain and heart.

summary: This unit covers how lymph is formed, how it moves, where it drains, and how lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, and mucosal lymphoid tissue are built. The exam asks about drainage routes, the zones of each lymphoid organ, and what goes wrong when lymph flow is blocked.

points: Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended tubes with overlapping endothelial cells that act as one-way flap valves.
Anchoring filaments hold them open when the tissue swells.
They return filtered fluid and leaked plasma protein to the blood, about 2 to 3 L per day.
Lacteals in intestinal villi take up dietary fat as chylomicrons, which makes lymph milky (chyle).
notes.why: Lymph forms because Starling forces leave a small net filtrate in the interstitium, and capillaries leak some albumin that has no other way back to the blood. When interstitial pressure rises, anchoring filaments tied to the surrounding matrix pull the endothelial flaps open so fluid and protein enter; when pressure inside the lymphatic rises, the flaps close and block backflow. Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries, so absorbed fat travels in lymph and joins the venous blood at the thoracic duct, bypassing the liver at first.

points: Collecting lymphatics have valves and smooth muscle that contract in segments (lymphangions).
Skeletal muscle contraction, breathing, nearby arterial pulsation, and outside compression all push lymph forward.
A rise in interstitial fluid pressure increases lymph flow, up to a maximum.
notes.why: Each lymphangion fills, stretches, and contracts, and its valves let lymph move only toward the next segment, so collecting lymphatics behave like a chain of small pumps. External compression from muscle, breathing, and arterial pulsation adds to this intrinsic pumping. Lymph flow rises steeply as interstitial pressure climbs from its normal slightly negative value, then levels off once tissue pressure rises a little above atmospheric, because that same pressure starts compressing the larger lymphatics.

points: Thoracic duct starts at the cisterna chyli (about L1 to L2), passes through the aortic hiatus, and drains into the left venous angle (left internal jugular and left subclavian junction).
Thoracic duct drains everything except the right upper body.
Right lymphatic duct (or its trunks separately) drains the right head, neck, arm, and right side of the thorax into the right venous angle.
notes.why: The thoracic duct starts in the abdomen, rises on the right of the aorta, crosses to the left at about T4 to T6, and ends at the left venous angle. That course explains the side of a chylothorax: injury below the crossing tends to give a right effusion and injury above it a left one. Because lymph from the abdomen passes through the thoracic duct, abdominal cancers such as gastric carcinoma can spread to the left supraclavicular (Virchow) node.

points: Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow (B cells mature) and thymus (T cells mature).
Secondary lymphoid organs: lymph nodes, spleen, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (tonsils, Peyer patches in the ileum, appendix).
Lymph node path: afferent vessels, subcapsular sinus, cortical sinuses, medullary sinuses, efferent vessel at the hilum.
Spleen filters blood: red pulp removes old red cells; white pulp mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens.
Thymus comes from the third pharyngeal pouch; positive selection happens in the cortex, negative selection in the medulla.
notes.why: A lymph node is built to bring antigen to lymphocytes: lymph percolates through the sinuses past macrophages and dendritic cells, B cells gather in cortical follicles, and T cells sit in the paracortex, where they enter from blood through high endothelial venules. The spleen has no afferent lymphatics and samples blood instead; red cells must squeeze through narrow slits in the red pulp, so stiff or aged cells are trapped and removed. In the thymus, cortical selection keeps T cells that recognize self MHC, and medullary selection, aided by AIRE, deletes those that bind self antigen strongly.

points: Lymphedema is protein-rich edema that becomes firm and nonpitting as fibrosis sets in.
Causes include lymph node removal or radiation (such as after breast cancer surgery), tumor, and filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti).
Thoracic duct injury leaks chyle into the pleural space (chylothorax).
notes.why: When lymph cannot drain, filtered protein stays in the interstitium, raises interstitial oncotic pressure, and holds more water, so the edema is rich in protein. The trapped protein drives chronic inflammation and fibroblast activity, and fibrosis with fat deposition makes the limb firm, nonpitting, and thick-skinned. In filariasis, adult worms live inside lymphatics, and the host inflammatory response damages and obstructs the vessels.

summary: This unit covers the physics of blood flow (pressure, resistance, viscosity, turbulence), the Starling forces that move fluid across capillaries, and how tissues control their own flow. Board questions ask you to predict what happens to flow or pressure when one variable changes.

points: Flow equals pressure difference divided by resistance (Q = ΔP / R).
For the whole circulation, mean arterial pressure is about cardiac output times total peripheral resistance.
Poiseuille: resistance = 8ηL / (πr⁴), so radius matters most.
Halving the radius raises resistance 16 times and cuts flow to one-sixteenth at the same pressure.
Resistances in series add; in parallel, 1/R total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + and so on, so the total is lower than any single branch.
Organs sit in parallel, which lets each one change its own flow without changing the others much.
notes.why: Because resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius, a small change in arteriolar radius changes resistance, and so flow, far more than a similar percentage change in driving pressure, which is why arterioles are the main resistance vessels and the main site of flow control. In a parallel network, each added bed lowers total resistance, so opening a capillary bed lowers total peripheral resistance and removing a parallel organ (as with a nephrectomy or amputation) raises it. Since mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance, pressure rises only when output or resistance rises.

points: Velocity = flow divided by total cross-sectional area, so blood moves slowest in capillaries.
Hematocrit is the main determinant of viscosity; polycythemia raises viscosity and resistance, anemia lowers them.
Turbulence becomes more likely with high velocity, low viscosity, large diameter, and rough or narrowed vessels (Reynolds number).
Turbulence makes bruits and murmurs, such as flow murmurs in anemia.
notes.why: Total cross-sectional area is greatest in the capillaries, so velocity is lowest there, which gives time for exchange. The Reynolds number rises with velocity, vessel diameter, and blood density and falls with viscosity; above a critical value laminar flow breaks into turbulence, which vibrates the wall and is heard as a bruit or murmur. Anemia lowers viscosity and raises velocity through a higher cardiac output, so a soft flow murmur can appear with normal valves.

points: Pulse pressure = systolic minus diastolic; it widens with stiff arteries or a larger stroke volume.
MAP is about diastolic pressure plus one-third of pulse pressure at resting heart rates.
Veins are about 24 times more compliant than their matching arteries and hold about 64% of blood volume.
Law of Laplace: wall tension rises with pressure and radius, so a dilated ventricle or aneurysm faces more wall stress.
notes.why: Compliance is the change in volume per change in pressure, so stiff arteries cannot buffer each stroke volume: systolic pressure climbs, diastolic pressure falls, and pulse pressure widens, as in isolated systolic hypertension of older adults. Mean pressure sits closer to diastolic because the heart spends about two-thirds of each cycle in diastole at rest. High venous compliance lets the veins act as a reservoir, and venoconstriction shifts that stored blood toward the heart to raise preload.

points: Starling: net filtration = Kf × [(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)].
Edema comes from higher capillary pressure, lower plasma oncotic pressure, leakier capillaries, or blocked lymphatics.
Lymph returns the small net filtrate and leaked protein to the blood.
Venous return is helped by venous valves, the skeletal muscle pump, and the drop in thoracic pressure during inspiration.
notes.why: Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out and plasma oncotic pressure, mostly from albumin, pulls it back; the reflection coefficient describes how well the wall holds back protein. Each cause of edema changes one term: heart failure raises capillary pressure, nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis lower plasma oncotic pressure, sepsis and burns make the wall leakier, and lymphatic obstruction removes the drain. Filtration normally exceeds reabsorption slightly, and lymph carries the difference back to the veins.

points: Metabolic control: adenosine, CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, lactate, and low O₂ dilate arterioles in active tissue.
Myogenic control: stretch of arteriolar smooth muscle triggers contraction, which keeps flow steady when pressure rises (autoregulation).
Endothelium releases nitric oxide (from shear stress) and prostacyclin to dilate, and endothelin to constrict.
Sympathetic nerves constrict most arterioles through α1 receptors.
Constrictors in blood: norepinephrine, angiotensin II, vasopressin. Dilators: bradykinin, histamine, ANP, nitric oxide.
Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X) report pressure to the nucleus of the solitary tract in the medulla.
notes.why: Local control matches flow to need: metabolites build up when flow falls short of demand and relax arterioles, while the myogenic response constricts a stretched arteriole and keeps flow steady across a range of pressures. Shear stress activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase; nitric oxide diffuses into smooth muscle, raises cGMP, lowers cytosolic calcium, and relaxes the vessel. Baroreceptors fire more as arterial walls stretch, and the medulla answers with more vagal and less sympathetic output, so heart rate, contractility, and arteriolar tone fall.

tricks.label: Radius to the fourth

pitfalls: Adding a parallel vascular bed lowers total resistance; adding a segment in series raises it.
Blood velocity is lowest in capillaries even though each capillary is tiny, because their combined area is the largest.
Pulmonary vessels constrict to hypoxia, the opposite of systemic vessels.
Higher hematocrit raises viscosity and resistance; anemia lowers them and favors turbulence.

summary: This unit covers how the heart and vessels respond during a single bout of exercise and how they adapt with regular training. Questions ask you to predict changes in heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, blood pressure, and resistance, and to tell an athlete's heart from disease.

points: Central command from the motor cortex and reflexes from muscle mechanoreceptors and metaboreceptors raise sympathetic output.
The early rise in heart rate comes from vagal withdrawal; sympathetic drive takes over as intensity rises.
Venoconstriction, the skeletal muscle pump, and deeper breathing push more blood back to the heart.
notes.why: Central command raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal outflow at the start of exercise, before metabolites accumulate, and reflexes from muscle mechanoreceptors and metaboreceptors add to the drive as contraction continues. Vagal withdrawal raises heart rate fastest because acetylcholine opens SA node potassium channels (IK,ACh) through G protein beta-gamma subunits without a second messenger, so its effect ends within a beat or two, while sympathetic effects work through cAMP and build over several seconds. Venoconstriction and the muscle pump move blood from the venous reservoir to the heart, raising preload so that cardiac output can rise.

points: Heart rate rises roughly in step with workload.
Stroke volume rises from more filling (Frank-Starling) and stronger contraction; in many untrained people it levels off at moderate intensity.
Cardiac output can rise about four- to fivefold in hard exercise in untrained adults, and more in trained endurance athletes.
Oxygen uptake follows the Fick principle: VO₂ = cardiac output × arteriovenous O₂ difference.
The arteriovenous O₂ difference widens because active muscle extracts more oxygen.
notes.why: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume; both rise early, and once stroke volume levels off, heart rate carries the further increase. The Fick equation shows two ways to raise oxygen uptake: deliver more blood or extract more oxygen from each liter, and exercise does both. Extraction rises because the low PO₂ in working muscle falls on the steep part of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, and high CO₂, acidosis, and heat shift the curve to the right, so hemoglobin releases more oxygen at any given PO₂.

points: Active muscle arterioles dilate to local metabolites (K⁺, adenosine, H⁺, CO₂, lactate) and nitric oxide.
Muscle blood flow can rise up to about 25 times in strenuous exercise.
Sympathetic constriction cuts flow to the gut, kidneys, and inactive muscle.
Skin flow rises as body temperature climbs, to shed heat.
Brain flow stays fairly constant; coronary flow rises with cardiac work.
notes.why: Metabolites in active muscle override sympathetic constriction there (functional sympatholysis), so flow concentrates in the working muscle while inactive beds stay constricted. Because the dilated muscle beds sit in parallel with the rest of the circulation, total peripheral resistance falls even though sympathetic tone rises elsewhere. As core temperature climbs, skin vessels dilate to shed heat, which competes with muscle for cardiac output during exercise in hot conditions.

notes.h: Blood pressure in two kinds of exercise
points: Dynamic (aerobic) exercise: systolic pressure rises, diastolic stays about the same or falls slightly, total peripheral resistance falls.
Static (isometric) exercise: contracting muscle squeezes its own vessels, so systolic and diastolic pressure both rise sharply.
Dynamic exercise is mainly a volume load on the heart; static exercise is mainly a pressure load.
notes.why: In dynamic exercise, systolic pressure rises because a larger stroke volume is ejected faster, while diastolic pressure stays about level because dilated muscle beds lower total peripheral resistance and let blood run off quickly. In static exercise, sustained contraction compresses the muscle's own vessels, metabolites accumulate, and the muscle metaboreflex drives a strong sympathetic pressor response while resistance stays high. That is why a heavy static effort is mainly a pressure load on the left ventricle, while running or cycling is mainly a volume load.

points: Endurance training enlarges the LV cavity with proportional wall thickening (eccentric remodeling), so stroke volume rises.
Plasma and blood volume increase, which raises preload.
Resting heart rate falls, mostly from higher vagal tone; maximum heart rate changes little.
Maximal cardiac output and VO₂max rise.
Trained muscle has more capillaries and mitochondria, so it extracts more oxygen.
Regular exercise lowers resting blood pressure, raises HDL, lowers triglycerides, and improves insulin sensitivity and endothelial nitric oxide release.
notes.why: Repeated volume loading adds sarcomeres in series, so the left ventricular cavity enlarges, holds more blood, and ejects a larger stroke volume. With a larger stroke volume, the same resting cardiac output needs fewer beats, and higher vagal tone lowers resting heart rate further. Peripheral gains, including more capillaries, mitochondria, and oxidative enzymes, widen the maximal arteriovenous O₂ difference, so VO₂max rises from both central and peripheral changes.

tricks.label: Run vs lift
tricks.text: Running opens muscle vessels, so resistance falls and diastolic pressure holds steady. Lifting squeezes them shut, so both systolic and diastolic pressure climb.

tricks.label: Big tank, slow pump
tricks.text: The trained heart has a bigger LV and more blood volume, so each beat moves more blood and the resting rate can be lower for the same output.

summary: This unit covers how lipids travel in the blood, how the heart makes its ATP, and which vitamins, minerals, and cofactors the heart and vessels depend on. The exam links a biochemical defect or deficiency to a heart or vessel problem, such as thiamine and high-output failure or homocysteine and thrombosis.

points: Exogenous path: intestine packs dietary triglyceride into chylomicrons (apo B-48), which reach the blood through lymph.
Lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium, activated by apo C-II, frees fatty acids from chylomicrons and VLDL.
Endogenous path: liver makes VLDL (apo B-100), which becomes IDL and then LDL as triglyceride is removed.
LDL delivers cholesterol to cells through the LDL receptor, which binds apo B-100.
HDL (apo A-I) carries cholesterol back to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport); apo A-I activates LCAT, which esterifies cholesterol.
CETP moves cholesteryl esters from HDL to VLDL, IDL, and LDL in exchange for triglyceride.
HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.
notes.why: Lipids are insoluble in plasma, so they travel in particles whose apolipoproteins act as address labels and enzyme switches: apo C-II turns on lipoprotein lipase, apo E and apo B-100 let remnants and LDL bind liver receptors, and apo A-I activates LCAT. As triglyceride is stripped from VLDL, the particle shrinks and becomes relatively richer in cholesterol, ending as LDL. Cells control uptake through the number of LDL receptors, which rises when cell cholesterol is low. Statins exploit this: by lowering hepatocyte cholesterol synthesis they activate SREBP, raise LDL receptor number, and pull more LDL out of plasma.

points: LDL that enters the intima can be oxidized; macrophages take it up through scavenger receptors that are not downregulated, becoming foam cells.
Lipoprotein(a) is an LDL-like particle with apo(a), which resembles plasminogen; its level is mostly genetic and it adds atherosclerotic risk.
Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL; omega-3 fatty acids (EPA, DHA) lower triglycerides at higher intakes.
notes.why: LDL crosses injured endothelium and is held by proteoglycans in the intima, where oxidation makes it a target for macrophage scavenger receptors. Because scavenger receptors are not turned down when the cell is full of cholesterol, macrophages keep taking up oxidized LDL until they become foam cells, which make up the fatty streak. Lipoprotein(a) adds risk by carrying cholesterol into the wall, and because apo(a) resembles plasminogen, it may also impair clot breakdown.

points: The adult heart at rest makes most of its ATP (roughly 60 to 90%) from fatty acid beta-oxidation; glucose, lactate, and ketones supply the rest.
Mitochondria fill about a third of cardiomyocyte volume, so the heart depends on a steady O₂ supply.
Long-chain fatty acids need carnitine and carnitine palmitoyltransferase I to enter mitochondria; malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I.
Creatine kinase moves high-energy phosphate from mitochondria to myofibrils as creatine phosphate.
In ischemia the heart switches to anaerobic glycolysis, lactate builds up, and contraction fails within a minute or two.
Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) carries electrons in the respiratory chain and is made from the same mevalonate pathway that statins block.
notes.why: Fatty acid oxidation yields more ATP per carbon than glucose but uses more oxygen per ATP, so the heart depends on uninterrupted coronary flow. Malonyl-CoA, made when glucose and insulin are plentiful, blocks CPT-I so the cell does not oxidize fatty acids while it is building them. In ischemia, oxidative phosphorylation stops, ATP falls, and anaerobic glycolysis produces lactate and H⁺; low ATP and acidosis stop contraction within about a minute.

points: Thiamine (B1), as thiamine pyrophosphate, is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase, and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase.
Thiamine deficiency with heart failure (wet beriberi) is a high-output state with dilated heart and peripheral vasodilation; risk is high in alcohol use disorder and malnutrition.
Homocysteine is remethylated to methionine by methionine synthase (needs B12 and folate) or converted to cystathionine by cystathionine beta-synthase (needs B6).
Deficiency of B12, folate, or B6 raises homocysteine, which injures endothelium and favors thrombosis.
Vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen; scurvy causes fragile vessels, bleeding gums, and perifollicular hemorrhage.
Vitamin K is needed to gamma-carboxylate factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S.
notes.why: Thiamine deficiency blocks pyruvate dehydrogenase, so pyruvate is diverted to lactate and ATP production falls; peripheral vasodilation lowers resistance and forces the heart to pump a high output until it fails. Homocysteine sits at a branch point, so losing any of its three B vitamin cofactors raises its level, and high homocysteine injures endothelium and favors thrombosis. Vitamins C and K are cofactors for post-translational changes: without vitamin C, collagen cannot form a stable triple helix, and without vitamin K, clotting factors cannot bind calcium on phospholipid surfaces.

points: Potassium (normal about 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L) sets resting membrane potential; both low and high levels cause arrhythmias.
Calcium (normal about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL) triggers contraction through L-type channels and calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Magnesium is needed for Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity; low magnesium increases renal potassium loss, so hypokalemia is hard to correct, and causes hypocalcemia by impairing PTH release and action.
Iron deficiency anemia causes a high-output, tachycardic state; iron overload (hemochromatosis) causes cardiomyopathy and conduction problems.
Selenium deficiency causes Keshan disease, a cardiomyopathy.
Copper is a cofactor for lysyl oxidase, which cross-links collagen and elastin; deficiency (as in Menkes disease) weakens arteries.
notes.why: The resting membrane potential sits near the potassium equilibrium potential, so hyperkalemia depolarizes cells and inactivates sodium channels (peaked T waves, then a wide QRS), while hypokalemia slows repolarization (flat T waves, U waves) and raises arrhythmia risk. Calcium entering through L-type channels during the plateau opens ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so contractility depends on calcium handling. Low intracellular magnesium removes its normal block on renal outer medullary potassium (ROMK) channels, so potassium keeps leaking into the urine until magnesium is replaced.

summary: This unit covers single-gene and chromosomal disorders that affect the heart and vessels, plus the gene-expression and cell-cycle ideas behind them. The exam asks you to match a gene or inheritance pattern to a cardiovascular finding and to explain the mechanism.

notes.h: Genetic principles seen in heart disease
points: Most single-gene cardiovascular disorders are autosomal dominant (familial hypercholesterolemia, HCM, Marfan, most long QT).
Variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance are common, so relatives with the same variant can look very different.
Locus heterogeneity: one disease, many genes (familial hypercholesterolemia from LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9; long QT from many channel genes).
Pleiotropy: one gene, many organs (fibrillin-1 in Marfan affects aorta, eye, and skeleton).
Gene dosage matters: familial hypercholesterolemia homozygotes are far more severe than heterozygotes.
Mitochondrial DNA disorders can cause cardiomyopathy and conduction block (for example Kearns-Sayre syndrome); heteroplasmy explains variable severity.
notes.why: Many cardiovascular disorders are dominant because one faulty copy is enough to cause disease, either by halving a protein dose that matters (haploinsufficiency, as with LDL receptors) or by making a mutant protein that disrupts the normal one (a dominant negative effect, as with fibrillin-1 in many Marfan cases). Penetrance and expressivity vary because modifier genes, sex, and environment change how a variant shows, so relatives need screening even when they look well. In mitochondrial disease the share of mutant mtDNA differs between tissues, and high-energy organs such as heart and muscle show disease once that share crosses a threshold.

points: Usually a mutation in the LDL receptor gene; APOB and gain-of-function PCSK9 variants cause the same picture.
Fewer working receptors means less LDL and IDL clearance, so more IDL becomes LDL.
Less cholesterol inside liver cells also takes the brake off cholesterol synthesis.
Heterozygotes have about two to three times normal plasma cholesterol; homozygotes about five to six times, often with MI before age 20.
Signs: tendon xanthomas (often Achilles), xanthelasma, early corneal arcus, premature coronary disease.
notes.why: Fewer LDL receptors slow the liver's removal of both IDL and LDL, so plasma LDL rises from poor clearance and from more IDL being converted to LDL. Inside liver cells, low cholesterol activates SREBP, which raises HMG-CoA reductase and cholesterol synthesis and adds to the load. Years of high LDL push cholesterol into tendons, eyelids, and the arterial intima, and homozygotes with almost no receptor function respond poorly to statins because statins lower LDL mainly by raising receptor number.

points: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: sarcomere protein genes, most often MYH7 (beta-myosin heavy chain) and MYBPC3 (myosin-binding protein C).
HCM shows myocyte disarray, asymmetric septal thickening, diastolic dysfunction, and a risk of sudden death in young athletes.
Congenital long QT comes from potassium channel loss (KCNQ1, KCNH2) or sodium channel gain (SCN5A), which delays repolarization and invites torsades de pointes.
Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is autosomal recessive long QT with sensorineural deafness; Romano-Ward syndrome is autosomal dominant without deafness.
Brugada syndrome: loss of function in SCN5A, ST elevation in V1 to V3 with a pseudo-right bundle branch block pattern, and sudden death risk.
Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy (dystrophin, X-linked) cause dilated cardiomyopathy; Friedreich ataxia (frataxin, GAA repeat) causes HCM.
notes.why: Mutant sarcomere proteins in HCM alter force generation and trigger hypertrophy with myocyte disarray, which stiffens the ventricle and forms a substrate for ventricular arrhythmias. Ventricular repolarization depends on outward potassium currents, so losing IKs (KCNQ1) or IKr (KCNH2), or keeping a late inward sodium current (SCN5A gain of function), prolongs the action potential and the QT interval. A long plateau allows early afterdepolarizations, which can trigger torsades de pointes and sudden death.

points: Marfan syndrome: FBN1 (fibrillin-1) on chromosome 15; faulty microfibrils weaken elastic tissue and increase TGF-beta signaling.
Marfan cardiovascular findings: aortic root dilation, aortic dissection, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1 or TGFBR2): aggressive aortic aneurysms, arterial tortuosity, bifid uvula, widely spaced eyes.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1, type III collagen): arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture.
notes.why: Fibrillin-1 forms microfibrils that scaffold elastic fibers and hold latent TGF-beta in the matrix, so defective fibrillin weakens the aortic media and frees more TGF-beta, which promotes matrix breakdown. The aortic root takes the highest pulsatile stress, so it dilates first, stretching the valve ring to cause aortic regurgitation and setting the stage for dissection. Loeys-Dietz variants in TGF-beta receptor genes involve the same pathway. Type III collagen gives tensile strength to arteries, bowel, and uterus, so its defect in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome leads to rupture of those organs.

notes.h: Gene expression and the cell cycle in the heart
points: Adult cardiomyocytes have largely left the cell cycle and renew very slowly, so dead myocardium is replaced by scar.
Under pressure or volume load, cardiomyocytes grow larger (hypertrophy) instead of dividing.
Hypertrophy reactivates fetal genes such as ANP, BNP, and beta-myosin heavy chain.
SREBP senses cell sterol levels and turns up LDL receptor and HMG-CoA reductase genes when cholesterol is low.
Smooth muscle cells in the intima proliferate in response to growth factors such as PDGF in atherosclerosis.
notes.why: Adult cardiomyocytes have largely left the cell cycle and renew very slowly, so they respond to load by adding sarcomeres rather than dividing, and an infarct heals with fibroblast scar rather than new muscle. Stretch and neurohormones such as angiotensin II, catecholamines, and endothelin switch on the fetal gene program, which is why BNP rises with ventricular wall stress and serves as a heart failure marker. SREBP is held in the endoplasmic reticulum when sterols are high and moves to the Golgi for cleavage when they are low, releasing a transcription factor that raises LDL receptor and HMG-CoA reductase expression.

tricks.text: Both can look tall and thin with a dislocated lens. Marfan lenses usually shift up and out; homocystinuria lenses shift down and in, and homocystinuria adds clots.

tricks.label: Receptor down, LDL up
tricks.text: In familial hypercholesterolemia, picture the liver with half its LDL receptors. LDL piles up in plasma, and the cell, sensing too little cholesterol inside, keeps making more.

highYield: Familial hypercholesterolemia is autosomal dominant; homozygotes can have MI before age 20.
MYH7 and MYBPC3 are the most common HCM genes; inheritance is autosomal dominant.
Marfan syndrome is caused by FBN1 mutations; aortic dissection is the main cause of death.
Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome: long QT plus sensorineural deafness, autosomal recessive.
Down syndrome is most linked to atrioventricular septal defects.
Turner syndrome is linked to bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation.
Williams syndrome causes supravalvular aortic stenosis through elastin gene loss.
Hypertrophied myocytes switch back on fetal genes such as ANP, BNP, and beta-myosin heavy chain.
pitfalls: Marfan (FBN1) and Loeys-Dietz (TGFBR1 or TGFBR2) both cause aortic aneurysm; Loeys-Dietz adds bifid uvula, widely spaced eyes, and arterial tortuosity.
Long QT from KCNQ1 and KCNH2 is a loss of potassium current, while SCN5A long QT is a gain of sodium current; Brugada is a loss of SCN5A function.
Cardiomyocytes respond to load by hypertrophy, while vascular smooth muscle cells can still proliferate.
Gain-of-function PCSK9 raises LDL; loss-of-function PCSK9 lowers it, because PCSK9 sends LDL receptors to be degraded.

flows.title: Pathogenesis of familial hypercholesterolemia
steps: LDLR mutation reduces functional hepatic LDL receptors.
Less LDL and IDL are cleared from plasma.
Low hepatocyte cholesterol activates SREBP and increases cholesterol synthesis.
Plasma LDL is high from birth.
LDL cholesterol deposits in tendons, skin, and the arterial intima.
Xanthomas and premature coronary artery disease develop.

flows.title: Marfan syndrome to aortic disease
steps: FBN1 mutation produces defective fibrillin-1.
Microfibrils fail to scaffold elastic fibers in the aortic media.
Less latent TGF-beta is held in matrix, so TGF-beta signaling increases.
Medial degeneration weakens the wall, most at the aortic root.
Root dilation causes aortic regurgitation and raises the risk of dissection.

flows.title: Congenital long QT to torsades de pointes
steps: KCNQ1 or KCNH2 loss of function reduces outward potassium current.
Ventricular repolarization is delayed and the QT interval lengthens.
A prolonged plateau lets L-type calcium channels reopen.
Early afterdepolarizations trigger premature ventricular beats.
Torsades de pointes can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.
